name: Darjeeling & Ghoom
tagline: The thunderbolt ridge, its tea and villages
meta_description: Darjeeling and Ghoom on a fair budget: toy train, Tiger Hill dawn, tea gardens, Tagore's Mungpoo and village homestays from ₹1,500 a night with meals.
summary: Darjeeling and Ghoom sit on a ridge at 2,000–2,260 m, 65 km above Siliguri. Come for the toy train, Kanchenjunga from Tiger Hill, Tibetan monasteries and the tea gardens, then stay a night or two in Lamahatta, Takdah or Chatakpur. A good trip costs ₹1,800–3,000 a day.

story.title: From Dorje-ling to the tea hills
paras: The name is usually traced to Tibetan: dorje, the thunderbolt sceptre of Buddhist ritual, and ling, a place. Local tradition holds that a small Buddhist shrine called Dorje-ling once stood on Observatory Hill, where Hindu and Buddhist priests today share the Mahakal temple. Before the British, this ridge belonged to the kingdom of Sikkim, was overrun by the Gorkhas of Nepal in the late 1700s, and was returned to Sikkim after the Anglo-Nepalese war. Its first people were the Lepcha, who call themselves Rong, or Rongkup, and whose names still mark many villages and rivers here.

In 1828 two East India Company officers, Captain George Lloyd and J. W. Grant, rode up to what they called the old Gorkha station of Dorjeling and saw a sanatorium in the cool air. On 1 February 1835 the Chogyal of Sikkim, Tsugphud Namgyal, signed a deed granting the hill to the Company. In 1839 Dr Archibald Campbell arrived as superintendent; around 1841 he planted China tea seeds in his garden at Beechwood. By 1852 the first commercial gardens, Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, were in production.

The railway reached the ridge in 1881 on track just 610 mm wide, and Ghoom, at 2,258 m, became its highest station. Nepali-speaking workers came in their thousands for the gardens and the roads, Bengali officials for the summer seat of government, and after 1959 Tibetan refugees, who founded the Self Help Centre on the Lebong road. Tenzing Norgay made Darjeeling his home, and the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute opened here in 1954. The hills around keep that mix: Lepcha, Nepali, Tibetan and Bengali, in one tea-scented district.

intro: Darjeeling is a town on a narrow ridge at about 2,042 m, with Ghoom, 7 km away and a little higher, as its gateway saddle. From Chowrasta you look north across the Rangeet valley to Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m. Most visitors give it two days: the toy train, Tiger Hill at dawn, the zoo and HMI, a tea garden. We think it rewards four or five.

Beyond the town, the land falls away in every direction into tea estates and villages that see few tourists: Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley on the Peshok road, Lepchajagat and Jorepokhri in the cryptomeria forest on the way to Mirik, Chatakpur inside the Senchal sanctuary, Mungpoo with its cinchona fields and Tagore's house, and Bijanbari down in the warm Rangeet valley.

This is a cheap part of the Himalaya to travel well. Shared jeeps link everything for ₹30–350 a seat, village homestays charge ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, and a plate of momos is under ₹150. What costs money is peak season in central Darjeeling, private cars and last-minute bookings. We show you how to avoid all three.

highlights.title: The toy train to Ghoom
highlights.text: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, a UNESCO World Heritage line since 1999, runs steam and diesel joyrides from Darjeeling round the Batasia Loop to Ghoom, its highest station at 2,258 m. Two hours, a small museum at Ghoom, and the Gorkha War Memorial in the middle of the loop.

highlights.title: Dawn at Tiger Hill
highlights.text: At 2,567 m, Tiger Hill catches first light on Kanchenjunga and, on very clear mornings, the far-off tip of Everest. Jeeps leave Darjeeling around 4 am. Below it lies the Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, declared in 1915, whose lakes still supply the town's water.

highlights.title: Yiga Choeling at Ghoom
highlights.text: Founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso, Ghoom's Gelug monastery keeps a seated Maitreya, the Buddha to come, about 4.6 m tall. Come for the morning prayers, then walk to Samten Choling and the Sakya monastery nearby, all within a short walk.

highlights.title: Tea where it started
highlights.text: Dr Archibald Campbell planted tea seeds in his Darjeeling garden around 1841. Walk to Happy Valley below the town, or stay in the gardens along the Peshok road, where Lopchu and Peshok estates roll down towards the Teesta. Plucking runs from March to November.

highlights.title: Tagore's Mungpoo
highlights.text: Rabindranath Tagore stayed four times between 1938 and 1940 in Maitreyi Devi's house among the cinchona plantations of Mungpoo, first planted by the government in 1864 to make quinine. The house is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum with his chairs, paintings and photographs.

highlights.title: Village nights for less
highlights.text: Sleep in Lamahatta under tall dhupi trees, in the old cantonment bungalows of Takdah, in Tinchuley's orange orchards, or in Chatakpur, a forest village of 19 houses inside the Senchal sanctuary. Homestays cost ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast.

getting_there: The railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the airport is Bagdogra, both on the edge of Siliguri, about 65–70 km and 3–3.5 hours below Darjeeling. Shared jeeps leave from the stands near the Siliguri bus terminus on Hill Cart Road and from outside NJP station when full, for about ₹250–350 a seat; in Darjeeling they stop around Chowk Bazaar and Clubside. A reserved small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹3,000–4,000, an SUV ₹3,500–5,000. The toy train climbs 88 km from NJP in 7–8 hours when the full line runs, which is not always: landslides often suspend it, so check current status before you travel. From Darjeeling, jeeps fan out to Ghoom, Sukhia Pokhari, Mirik, Kalimpong, Gangtok and Maneybhanjan from the Chowk Bazaar motor stand. Leave Siliguri by early afternoon to arrive before dark.
permits: No permits are needed for the Darjeeling hills for Indian or foreign visitors. Chatakpur and Tiger Hill lie in or beside the Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, where small entry and vehicle fees apply and Chatakpur homestays collect the forest department's entry fee on your behalf. If you continue to Sikkim, foreign nationals need an Inner Line Permit, issued at the border checkposts or online; Singalila National Park, for Sandakphu, requires a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a shoestring, ₹1,500–2,000 a day covers a hostel bed or shared room, momos and thalis, and shared jeeps; Darjeeling town has dorm beds for about ₹400–700. A comfortable budget of ₹2,500–3,500 buys a central budget-hotel room or a village homestay with meals, a reserved car for the Tiger Hill dawn trip (₹1,500–2,200 a car) and a toy train joyride (roughly ₹1,000–1,800). People overspend in three places: peak-season rooms on the Mall booked late, private cars for trips a shared jeep would do, and packaged 'sightseeing points' tours that add little. Homestays outside town are better value than Darjeeling hotels in October and May.

months.weather: Darjeeling 2–9 °C, dry, clear mornings, frost at Ghoom and Tiger Hill
months.summary: The coldest month and one of the clearest. Kanchenjunga often stands out all morning, crowds are thin after New Year week, and hotel rates fall. Nights near freezing make old buildings cold, so ask for heaters. Village homestays at Lamahatta and Chatakpur are bitter at night but quiet. A good month for photographers and couples who pack warm and do not mind short days.
months.tip: Book a room with a heater and pack a down jacket; Tiger Hill at 5 am is well below freezing.

months.summary: Still cold, a little longer in the day, and usually clear. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, often falls this month, and the Ghoom monasteries fill with families offering khatas and butter lamps. Off-season prices hold until early March. Rhododendrons start to bud on the higher slopes late in the month. A calm, cheap month for monasteries, the toy train and town walks.
months.tip: Ask a monastery or your hotel for the year's Losar date; it moves with the lunar calendar.

months.weather: Darjeeling 7–15 °C, dry, some haze late in the month
months.summary: Spring arrives: first-flush tea plucking begins in the gardens, magnolias and rhododendrons bloom in the forests around Lepchajagat and Tiger Hill, and mornings are often clear. The orchid centre at Takdah is at its best from February to April. Prices are moderate before the April–June rush. A fine month for village stays and tea garden walks.
months.tip: Visit a garden in the first-flush weeks and taste the new tea at the source, light and green.

months.weather: Darjeeling 10–17 °C, mostly dry, afternoon cloud and haze
months.summary: Warm days and cool nights, rhododendrons in flower, and good mornings for Kanchenjunga before haze builds by noon. Tea gardens are busy with plucking. School holidays in the plains begin towards the end of the month and prices start to climb in Darjeeling town. Village homestays on the Peshok road and the Ghoom–Mirik road stay calm and fairly priced.
months.tip: Plan viewpoints for dawn; by 10 am April haze often hides the peaks.

months.weather: Darjeeling 12–19 °C, warm days, pre-monsoon showers late in the month
months.summary: Peak season. Families from the plains fill Darjeeling, the toy train joyrides sell out and room rates are at their highest. Mornings can still be clear, and evenings pleasant. Mungpoo marks Tagore's birthday on 25 Baishakh, usually 8 or 9 May. Escape the Mall crowds by staying in Takdah, Tinchuley or Lepchajagat and visiting town for a day.
months.tip: Book toy train joyrides on IRCTC weeks ahead for May and June.

months.weather: Darjeeling 14–19 °C, monsoon arriving mid-month, heavy afternoon rain
months.summary: The first half of June is still busy with school holidays; by mid-month the monsoon arrives, the crowds thin, and views mostly vanish into cloud. The second flush tea, the muscatel that made Darjeeling famous, is plucked from late May into June. Roads begin to see landslides. Good for tea lovers and anyone who likes mist and green hills at lower prices.
months.tip: Carry an umbrella and leech socks for village walks from mid-June.

months.weather: Darjeeling 15–19 °C, heavy rain most days, landslides
months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Rain falls most days, roads are often blocked for hours by landslides, the full toy train line is frequently suspended, and views are rare. Prices drop sharply and the hills are bright green. Only come if you are flexible, have buffer days, and are happy with cafés, monasteries and misty walks.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before any train or flight out of NJP or Bagdogra.

months.summary: Much like July: heavy rain, slips on the hill roads and short clear spells. Homestays and hotels offer their lowest rates of the year, and the tea gardens are in monsoon flush. Avoid remote villages like Chatakpur, whose forest track turns rough. Stay central, enjoy the quiet town, and watch the weather before any day trip.
months.tip: Check road status every morning with your hotel before setting off on a day trip.

months.weather: Darjeeling 14–18 °C, rain easing, clearer by month's end
months.summary: The monsoon fades through the month and the first clear mornings return towards the end. Prices are still low until Dashain and the Bengali Puja holidays, which in some years begin in late September and bring the autumn rush. A good month for value if you can travel early, with green hills and fewer people.
months.tip: If the Puja holidays fall in late September, book rooms well before the month starts.

months.summary: The best month for views, and the busiest. The air is washed clean after the monsoon and Kanchenjunga is visible most mornings. Dashain and Durga Puja, then Tihar, fill the hills with visitors and with festival life. Book rooms, jeeps and toy train seats early, and consider a village base such as Tinchuley or Lepchajagat to avoid the town's crowds.
months.tip: Book the Tiger Hill dawn trip for a weekday; weekends in October are crowded.

months.summary: Clear, crisp and calmer than October once the festival weeks pass. Tihar's lamps and Deusi singing come early in the month in many years. This is our favourite month for Tiger Hill, Chatakpur and the Lepchajagat forest, with steady views and lower prices. Evenings are cold, so pack warm, and expect autumn-flush tea in the gardens.
months.tip: Pack warm layers: November nights fall to 4–6 °C in town and colder in the villages.

months.summary: Cold, clear and cheaper, until the Christmas and New Year week, when Darjeeling fills with visitors from Kolkata and prices rise. The town's churches hold Christmas services and the Mall is lit up. Early in the month is one of the best windows of the year for mountain views, with thin crowds. Frost at Ghoom and Tiger Hill.
months.tip: Come in the first half of December for clear views at off-season prices.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Three nights in Darjeeling covers the toy train, Tiger Hill at dawn, Ghoom's monasteries, the zoo and HMI, and a tea garden walk. Add one or two nights in a village such as Lamahatta, Takdah or Chatakpur for quiet and better value. A week lets you add Mungpoo and the Ghoom–Mirik road without rushing.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to reach Darjeeling from NJP?
faqs.a: A shared jeep, at about ₹250–350 a seat, from the stand outside NJP station or the stands near the Siliguri bus terminus on Hill Cart Road. Jeeps leave when full and take 3–3.5 hours. The toy train is slower and dearer in first class, and the full line is often suspended, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: October to early December gives the clearest views of Kanchenjunga, with October busiest because of the festival holidays. March to May brings spring flowers and first-flush tea but more haze and crowds in May. July and August are wet, cheap and often cut off by landslides. December and January are cold but very clear.

faqs.q: How much does a Darjeeling trip cost per day?
faqs.a: About ₹1,500–2,000 a day on a shoestring with dorm beds, shared jeeps and local food; ₹2,500–3,500 with a budget hotel or homestay with meals, a toy train joyride and the Tiger Hill dawn trip; more in peak weeks. Village homestays at ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals are the best value in the district.

faqs.q: Is the Tiger Hill sunrise worth it?
faqs.a: On a clear morning, yes: first light moves down Kanchenjunga's face, and you may see Everest far to the west. It means a 4 am start, cold, and crowds in October and May. Go on a clear forecast, ideally on a weekday, and add Ghoom monastery and Batasia Loop on the way back.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Darjeeling?
faqs.a: No. Indian and foreign visitors need no permit for Darjeeling and the villages around it. Small entry fees apply at Tiger Hill, the zoo and HMI, Batasia Loop and the Senchal sanctuary area, including Chatakpur. Foreigners going on to Sikkim need an Inner Line Permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which toy train ride should I take?
faqs.a: Most visitors take a joyride from Darjeeling to Ghoom and back, about two hours with stops at Batasia Loop and the Ghoom museum. Steam joyrides cost roughly ₹1,500–1,800 and diesel ones roughly ₹1,000–1,300. The full NJP–Darjeeling run takes 7–8 hours when it operates. Book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for a quiet trip near Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Choose a village base: Lamahatta or Takdah and Tinchuley on the Peshok road, Lepchajagat on the Mirik road, or Chatakpur inside the Senchal sanctuary. Homestays there charge about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. In town, the ridge-top lanes such as Dr Zakir Hussain Road are calmer than the market.

faqs.q: Is Darjeeling good for a family trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Distances are short, the toy train, zoo, HMI, ropeway and Batasia Loop suit children, and food is simple and familiar. Keep to two bases, avoid long drives after lunch, and book rooms with heaters from November to February. Steep lanes can tire grandparents, so hire short taxi hops.
